'''Isabella Helen Mary Muir''' [[Commander of the Order of the British Empire|CBE]] [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] (20 August 1920 – 28 November 2005) was a British [[biochemist]]. She did pioneering work on the causes of [[osteoarthritis]].

==Personal life==

===Early life===
Muir was born in India to G. B. F. (Basil) Muir and Gladys Helen Mary, and spent the first 10 years of her life there.<ref name=ODNB/> Until moving to Europe in 1930, Muir had no formal education and was educated by her mother.<ref name="Hardingham">{{cite web|last=Hardingham|first=Tim|title=Helen Muir|url=http://www.biochemist.org/bio/02803/0062/028030062.pdf|accessdate=2 November 2013}}</ref> At the age of 10, Muir began her general education at a boarding school in [[Montreux]], Switzerland and at the [[Downe House School|Downe House]] in Berkshire, England. She began attending [[Somerville College, Oxford|Somerville College]] in Oxford, England in 1940, with the original intentions of studying medicine. However, under the influence of her tutor, [[Dorothy Hodgkin]], she switched her area of focus to chemistry. She graduated in 1944 with a [[bachelor's degree|second-class degree]].<ref name=ODNB/> She then went on to earn her Doctor of Philosophy in 1947 for a thesis on the chemical synthesis of penicillin – the supply of penicillin to stop wound infection was of high priority, as she did her research during World War II.<ref name= Hardingham/>

===Adult life===

Muir, a "fiery redhead", never married.<ref name=ODNB>{{cite ODNB|last=Hardingham|first=Tim|title=Muir, (Isabella) Helen Mary|url=http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/96567|year=2004|doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/96567|accessdate=2 November 2013}}</ref> The year after she earned her PhD, she worked as a research fellow at the [[Sir William Dunn School of Pathology]] at the University of Oxford.<ref name="ABC-CLIO">{{cite book|last1=Stevens|first1=Catherine M. C. Haines with Helen M.|title=International women in science : a biographical dictionary to 1950|date=2001|publisher=ABC-CLIO|location=Santa Barbara, Calif. [u.a.]|isbn=978-1576070901|page=[https://archive.org/details/internationalwom00hain/page/216 216]|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/internationalwom00hain/page/216}}</ref> [[Albert Neuberger]] then recruited her into a new group in London in the biochemical division of the [[National Institute for Medical Research]], and she moved to [[Mill Hill]] in 1949.<ref name="ABC-CLIO"/> Muir's interests shifted to biology under Neuberger, as he was studying the origin of haem biosynthesis. Muir published her first major papers with Neuberger in the [[Biochemical Journal]] in 1949 and 1950 on the [[biogenesis]] of [[porphyrin]]s.<ref name= Hardingham/> This initial work led to Muir's interest in collagen and human connective tissues. 
She was awarded an Empire Rheumatism Fellowship with research space at St. Mary's Medical School in London.<ref name= Hardingham/>
For most of Muir's career, she worked at the Kennedy Institute of Rheumatology in [[Hammersmith]], the world's first specialist rheumatology institute. 
She was recruited to head a research division at The Kennedy Institute in 1966.<ref name= Hardingham/> During her time at the Institute, she published papers in the [[Biochemical Journal]] and Nature.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Muir|first1=Helen|title=Chemistry of a Mucopolysaccharide produced by Guinea Pig Lymphocytes|journal=Nature|volume=191|date=12 August 1961|issue=4789|page=706|doi=10.1038/191706a0|pmid=13773630|bibcode=1961Natur.191..706M|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Tsiganos|first1=CP|title=Studies on Protein-Polysaccharides from Pig Laryngeal Cartilage EXTRACTION AND PURIFICATION|journal=Biochemical Journal|date=30 January 1969|volume=113|issue=5|pages=879–884|doi=10.1042/bj1130879|pmid=4241780|pmc=1184779|url=http://www.biochemj.org/bj/113/0879/1130879.pdf|accessdate=14 October 2014}}</ref> 
She then went on to become the Institute's director in 1977, the same year she was one of only a few women made a Fellow of the Royal Society.<ref name= ODNB/><ref name="Obituary: Helen Muir">{{cite news|last1=Richmond|first1=Caroline|title=Obituary: Helen Muir|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2006/jan/04/obituaries.obituaries|accessdate=14 October 2014|work=The Guardian|date=4 January 2006}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Stevens|first1=Catherine M. C. Haines with Helen M.|title=International women in science : a biographical dictionary to 1950|date=2001|publisher=ABC-CLIO|location=Santa Barbara, Calif. [u.a.]|isbn=978-1576070901|page=[https://archive.org/details/internationalwom00hain/page/216 216]|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/internationalwom00hain/page/216}}</ref><ref>Hardingham, Tim (2018). "Isabella Helen Mary Muir CBE. 20 August 1920—28 November 2005". ''[[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]]''. [[doi:10.1098/rsbm.2017.0042]]</ref> 
Muir's group at the Kennedy Institute worked discovering the structure and functions of [[proteoglycan]]s, proteins that make up a large part of cartilage.<ref name= Hardingham/>
She is largely credited with discovering and exploring the varied causes of [[osteoarthritis]] and with illuminating the biochemical causes of the condition, which had previously been considered unworthy of study.<ref name="Obituary: Helen Muir"/>
Muir retired from the Kennedy Institute in 1990.<ref name= ODNB/>

===Later life and death===

Muir retired to [[Yorkshire]], where her interest in science and medicine continued. She added solar panelling to her house and worked to preserve the habitats of local wildlife. After battling breast cancer for several years, she died on 28 November 2005 in her home near [[Bedale]], Yorkshire.<ref name= ODNB/>
